claims.text: The baseline is an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin coating on a conventional metal substrate.
Annealing at approximately 300–400°C promotes Cu diffusion in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Annealing-driven Cu diffusion causes Cu to segregate to the coating surface.
Annealing produces a Cu-rich surface layer and/or a modified Cu-associated oxide film.
The Cu-rich surface phase acts as a lubricious interlayer.
The Cu-rich interlayer reduces direct metal–metal contact and lowers interfacial shear during sliding.
Lower interfacial shear caused by the Cu-rich layer reduces friction.
Lower interfacial shear caused by the Cu-rich layer reduces coating wear.
Thermally altered surface chemistry changes microscopic deformation from brittle cracking toward ductile deformation.
The ductile microscopic deformation is dominated by dislocation glide and shear.
Relative to the as-deposited coating, the annealed coating will have a lower coefficient of friction during high-temperature sliding.
Relative to the as-deposited coating, the annealed coating will have a lower wear volume or wear rate during high-temperature sliding.
The annealed coating will show greater Cu enrichment at the surface than the as-deposited coating.
The annealed coating will show more ductile shear deformation and less brittle cracking than the as-deposited coating.
The proposed mechanism operates during sliding near 300–400°C because this regime provides sufficient thermal activation for Cu diffusion.
At lower temperatures, insufficient Cu migration may prevent formation of the lubricious surface phase.
The hypothesis is falsified if annealing produces no statistically significant friction or wear reduction, no surface Cu enrichment, and no deformation-mode change under otherwise identical tests.
